reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: A panocular developmental disorder, usually autosomal dominant, caused by heterozygous mutations or deletions of the PAX6 gene on chromosome 11p13
Characterised by partial or near-complete absence of the iris, though the underlying problem affects the whole eye, not just the iris
Associated features include foveal and optic nerve hypoplasia, nystagmus, photophobia, and reduced visual acuity from birth
Aniridia-associated keratopathy from limbal stem cell deficiency, cataract, and glaucoma are important vision-threatening complications that develop over time
Sporadic aniridia due to larger 11p13 deletions can involve the adjacent WT1 gene, causing WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, range of intellectual disability)
Children with sporadic aniridia require renal ultrasound surveillance for Wilms tumour until the risk period has passed and WT1 involvement is excluded
Lifelong monitoring for glaucoma and keratopathy is essential, and coloured or occlusive contact lenses can reduce glare and photophobia
reference.pathophysiology: Aniridia results from haploinsufficiency of PAX6, a master transcription factor that orchestrates development of the eye and parts of the central nervous system and pancreas. Reduced PAX6 dosage disrupts formation of multiple ocular structures, producing iris hypoplasia together with foveal and optic nerve hypoplasia, and predisposing to limbal stem cell deficiency, cataract, and abnormal anterior chamber angle development. The result is a spectrum of structural and functional deficits present from birth. In sporadic cases caused by contiguous gene deletions of 11p13, loss of the neighbouring WT1 tumour-suppressor gene confers a high risk of Wilms tumour, defining the WAGR association.
additionalDifferentials: Traumatic iridodialysis or surgical iris loss
Iridocorneal endothelial syndrome and other iris atrophies
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination documenting iris and corneal surface status
Intraocular pressure measurement and gonioscopy for glaucoma
Optical coherence tomography assessing foveal hypoplasia
Molecular testing for PAX6 mutations and 11p13 deletion analysis
Renal ultrasonography surveillance for Wilms tumour in sporadic cases
Paediatric and genetic assessment for WAGR features
redFlags: New or uncontrolled raised intraocular pressure indicating glaucoma
Progressive corneal opacification from limbal stem cell deficiency
Abdominal mass, haematuria, or genitourinary anomaly suggesting Wilms tumour in sporadic aniridia
reference.prognosis: Visual acuity is typically reduced from birth due to foveal hypoplasia and often declines further with progressive glaucoma, cataract, and keratopathy; prognosis in WAGR cases is additionally determined by the outcome of Wilms tumour.
pitfalls: Treating aniridia as an isolated iris defect and missing the panocular and systemic implications
Failing to arrange Wilms tumour surveillance in a child with apparently sporadic aniridia
Overlooking insidious glaucoma or progressive keratopathy on routine review
Not offering genetic counselling given the dominant inheritance and reproductive risk
management: Optimise residual vision with cycloplegic refraction and correction of refractive error, amblyopia therapy in childhood, and tinted or UV-protective lenses for photophobia
Protect the ocular surface in aniridia-associated keratopathy with intensive lubrication and, in advanced limbal stem cell deficiency, limbal stem cell or ocular surface transplantation
Screen for and treat glaucoma with intraocular-pressure-lowering drops, escalating to surgery when medical control is inadequate
Undertake cataract surgery cautiously when the lens opacity becomes visually significant
Maintain renal ultrasound surveillance for Wilms tumour in sporadic 11p13-deletion cases until the risk period has passed and WT1 involvement is excluded
Provide low-vision aids and educational support alongside multidisciplinary follow-up with ophthalmology, paediatrics, and oncology where WAGR features exist
Offer genetic counselling with PAX6 and 11p13 deletion testing and family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance
